An introduction to advanced microbiology techniques including molecular biology, parasitology, and virology is explored. 30 hours of clinical placement
prerequisites: MEDLABSC 2MS3  and registration in the MLS diploma program

name: Clinical Microbiology Simulation
description: This course involves laboratory isolation, identification and reporting of microorganisms from clinical specimens originating from a range of body sites. It is at an advanced level of understanding and interpretation which is intended to introduce standard techniques and methodologies used to identify common pathogens in a routine clinical microbiology laboratory. Laboratory safety, Quality control and quality assurance are incorporated. Labs (4 hours)
prerequisites: MEDLABSC 1S03  and registration in the MLS diploma program

name: Histotechnology Practicum
description: Students who successfully complete this course will perform processing, embedding, decalcification, section cutting biological staining and cover slipping working independently and as part of the laboratory team. The student will critically evaluate the blocks and slides produced and repeat those which are not of diagnostic quality. 30 hours of clinical placement
prerequisites: MEDLABSC 1PS3  and registration in the MLS diploma program

name: Molecular Diagnostics Simulation Lab
description: This clinical simulation course explores the emerging field of molecular diagnostics through a molecular biology lens. It will expand upon material covered in previous courses and allow students an opportunity to manipulate DNA and RNA in a simulated laboratory setting. Topics will include an overview of molecular biology, common and emerging molecular biology methods including both manual and automated techniques, and an overview of molecular diagnostics. Labs (4 hours)
prerequisites: MEDLABSC 1A03  and registration in the MLS diploma program

name: Transfusion Medicine Practicum
description: This course provides experience in analyzing and interpreting laboratory results, employing safe practices in clinical laboratories, communicating and collaborating with the clinical programs which interface with the laboratory, and understanding and applying concepts in quality management. Students will perform investigations of prenatal and pre-transfusion testing, along with post-natal, post transfusion, and cord blood testing. 30 hours of clinical placement
prerequisites: MEDLABSC 2TS3  and registration in the MLS diploma program

name: Transfusion Medicine Simulation lab
description: The course will introduce students to a simulated clinical experience in a Transfusion Science laboratory. The knowledge and skills obtained in the Introduction to TM and Blood Bank course will be applied to real-life situations. Prenatal and pre-transfusion testing is performed along with associated investigations of atypical human blood group antibodies. Labs (4 hours)
prerequisites: MEDLABSC 1TM3  and registration in the MLS diploma program

name: Introductory Microeconomics
description: An introduction to the method and theory of microeconomics, and their application to the analysis of contemporary economic problems. In-class and online; one tutorial; one term

name: Introductory Macroeconomics
description: An introduction to the method and theory of macroeconomics, and their application to the analysis of contemporary economic problems. In-class and online; one tutorial; one term

name: Introduction to Mathematical Economics
description: This course is an introduction to mathematical and statistical methods applied in economics. It will improve the mathematical skills required to study intermediate economic theories and analyze economic data. Topics include partial derivatives, optimization, basic probability and statistics, and linear algebra. The mathematical results are illustrated through fundamental economic applications. Three hours, one tutorial; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Economics I; Social Sciences 1
Honours Health and Society 1
or in level 2 of any Social Sciences program; completion of Grade 12 Calculus or MATH 1F03 . Not open to students with credit or registration in MATH 1A03
1MM3
1LS3
1ZA3
restrictions: Not open to students with credit or registration in MATH 1A03 , 1M03, 1MM3 , 1LS3 , 1X03 , 1ZA3 .

name: Economics of Labour-Market Issues
description: This course applies economic analysis to issues of importance in the labour market. Topics vary and may include: women in the Canadian labour market; discrimination in hiring and promotion; unemployment; job loss and workplace closing; work sharing. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 1B03
1BX3  or ARTSSCI 2E03
restrictions:
Antirequisite(s): LABRST 3A03
Not open to students with credit or registration in ECON 3D03 .

name: Analysis of Economic Data
description: Application of statistical concepts to the analysis of economic data, with attention to Canadian sources. Regression analysis and the use of spreadsheets are included. Topics may also include index numbers. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 1B03
1BX3 and one of ECON 1BB3
1BA3; or ARTSSCI 2E03 ; and one of ECON 1ME3
COMMERCE 1DA3
STATS 1L03
STATS 1LL3
or Grade 12 Mathematics of Data Management U
or permission of the department
restrictions:
Antirequisite(s): COMMERCE 2QA3 , ENVSOCTY 3MB3 , GEOG 3MB3
Not open to students with credit or registration in ARTSSCI 2R03 , CHEMENG 4C03, ELECENG 3TQ4, HTHSCI 2A03, MATLS 3J03 , POLSCI 3N06 A/B, 3NN3 , PNB 2XE3 , 3XE3 , SOCIOL 3H06 A/B, STATS 2B03 , 2D03 , 2MB3 , 3Y03 .
Not open to students enrolled in any Business 1 or Bachelor of Commerce program.

name: Health Economics and its Application to Health Policy
description: Economic analysis of health and health care, with a special emphasis on policy issues in the Canadian health care system. Three hours (lectures and discussion); one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above
restrictions: Not open to students registered in an Economics program or with credit or registration in ECON 2Z03 , or ECON 3Z03 .

name: Economic Issues
description: Applications of economics to important public issues, from a general interest perspective. Since topics vary from year to year, interested students should consult the Economics Department for further details. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 1B03
1BX3  and one of ECON 1BB3
1BA3; or ARTSSCI 2E03

name: Financial Economics
description: Detailed investigation of the financial sector. Topics include the role of capital markets in facilitating investment and growth, bond markets, stock markets, financial statements and taxation. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 1B03
1BX3  and one of ECON 1BB3
1BA3; or ARTSSCI 2E03
restrictions:
Not open to students with credit or registration in COMMERCE 2FA3 .
Not open to students enrolled in any Business 1 or Bachelor of Commerce program.

name: Environmental Economics
description: Allocation of environmental services: efficiency and market failure; measuring environmental benefits; environmental regulation in Canada and elsewhere: taxes, tradable permits and other instruments; further topics. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 1B03
1BX3
or ARTSSCI 2E03

name: Economic History of Canada
description: A survey of the changing structure of the Canadian economy from the colonial period to the present; early significance of primary production for export markets; emerging domestic markets and industrialization; government’s role in promoting the development of the national economy. Fully online; one term
prerequisites: ECON 1B03  (or 1BX3) and one of ECON 1BB3
1BA3; or ARTSSCI 2E03

name: Macroeconomic Policy
description: This course integrates both theoretical foundations and practical applications of macroeconomic policy. While the course is grounded in standard macroeconomic theory, it emphasizes the practical applications of macroeconomic policy as they affect macro variables such as interest rates, employment, and inflation. Three hours, one term.
prerequisites: One of ECON 1BB3
1BA3
or ARTSSCI 2E03 ; and one of MATH 1K03  or Grade 12 Advanced Functions U. Students without credit in one of MATH 1F03
Grade 12 Calculus and Vectors U (or Grade 12 Advanced Functions and Introductory Calculus U) or equivalent are strongly advised to register in MATH 1F03  or MATH 1M03
1MM3  concurrently with ECON 2Y03

name: Public Policy Toward Business
description: The economic effects of federal competition policy and the regulation of business by all levels of government. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 1B03
1BX3; or ARTSSCI 2E03

name: Economics of Professional Sports
description: The application of economic principles to team and individual professional sports. Theory of sports leagues, demand for sports, the market for athletes, broadcasting rights, competition policy issues, the public finance aspects of stadium financing. Fully online; one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 1B03
1BX3; or ARTSSCI 2E03

name: Economics of Trade Unionism and Labour
description: Topics include the economics of the labour market, of trade unionism, of work, the impact of trade unions on the labour market, economic theories of strikes and trade unions and the state. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 1B03
1BX3  or ARTSSCI 2E03

name: Intermediate Macroeconomics I
description: This course uses macroeconomic theory based on microeconomic underpinnings to study common topics, including consumption-savings decisions, business cycles and economic growth. Three hours, one term.
prerequisites: One of ECON 1BB3
1BA3
or ARTSSCI 2E03 ; and one of MATH 1K03  or Grade 12 Advanced Functions U. Students without credit in one of MATH 1F03
Grade 12 Calculus and Vectors U (or Grade 12 Advanced Functions and Introductory Calculus U) or equivalent are strongly advised to register in MATH 1F03  or MATH 1M03
MATH 1MM3  concurrently with ECON 2Y03

name: Intermediate Macroeconomics II
description: This course builds on ECON 2Y03 , exploring advanced topics such as credit market imperfections, search and unemployment, monetary models, banking, and the open economy. Three hours, one term.
prerequisites: ECON 2Y03

name: Intermediate Microeconomics I
description: Theory of consumer choice; elements of production and cost; price and output determination in perfectly competitive markets. Three hours; one tutorial; one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 1B03  (or 1BX3 )
1BA3 (or 1BB3 )
or ARTSSCI 2E03 ; and credit or registration in ECON 1ME3
or completion of one of MATH 1A03
1LS3
or 1M03 or 1MM3  (or equivalent such as ARTSSCI 1D06 A/B
MATH 1N03
or 1ZA3 )

name: Intermediate Microeconomics II
description: Firm and consumer behaviour in imperfectly competitive markets and the markets for factors of production; the role of taxes and subsidies; theory of exchange, welfare economics and general equilibrium analysis. May include other special topics. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03 ; and one of ECON 1ME3
MATH 1A03
1LS3
or 1MM3  (or equivalent such as ARTSSCI 1D06 A/B
MATH 1N03
or 1ZA3 )

name: Public Sector Economics: Expenditures
description: Theory and practice of public finance. Topics are selected from growth of the public sector, market failure, theory of public goods, incentive mechanisms, logic of group decisions and the political process, theory of benefit-cost analysis, intergovernmental fiscal relations, government budgeting. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03

name: Behavioural Economics
description: Economic theory rests upon the assumptions that all economic actors (consumers, firms, governments) are fully rational and narrowly self-interested. Behavioural economics examines the consequences and realism of these assumptions by designing laboratory and field experiments and conducting empirical analyses that test economic theory and its core assumptions and by incorporating psychologically plausible assumptions and motivations into economic theory. This course provides a survey of some of the central and current topics in behavioural economics. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03

name: Public Sector Economics: Taxation
description: Theory and practice of public finance: analysis and comparison of the efficiency, equity and distribution effects of the taxation of income, wealth and expenditure, analysis of social insurance, intergovernmental fiscal relations. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03

name: Labour Economics
description: Introduction to the economics of the labour market; demand for labour by the firm and industry; supply of labour by the individual; investment in human capital. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03
restrictions: Not open to students with credit or registration in ECON 2A03 .

name: Applied Econometrics
description: Students acquire hands-on experience, using statistical software, in the application of econometric methods to empirically analyze economic issues. This course emphasizes understanding economic data, economic model estimation, hypothesis testing, and interpretation of results. Three hours; one tutorial; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03 ; and 2H03 or 2Y03 ; and 2B03  and enrolment in an Honours Economics program
restrictions:
Antirequisite(s): ECON 3EE3 , ECON 2B03  may be substituted with one of CHEMENG 4C03, COMMERCE 2QA3 , POLSCI 3N06 A/B, 3NN3 , PNB 2XE3 , 3XE3 , SOCIOL 3H06 A/B, STATS 2D03  or another course that is approved by a departmental counselor as equivalent to ECON 2B03 .
Not open to students with credit in STATS 2MB3 , 3D03 or credit or registration in ECON 4G03 .

name: Econometrics I
description: Elaboration of regression techniques developed in ECON 2B03 and their applications. Problems of inference and interpretation in the analysis of economic data. Introduction to forecasting in economics. Three lectures; one tutorial; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03 ; and 2H03 or 2Y03 ; and 2B03  with a grade of at least B-; and a GPA of at least 6. The ECON 2B03  prerequisite can be met by getting a grade of at least B+ in one of the following alternative statistics courses: ARTSSCI 2R03
CHEMENG 4C03
COMMERCE 2QA3
POLSCI 3N06 A/B
POLSCI 3NN3
PNB 2XE3
3XE3
SOCIOL 3H06 A/B
STATS 2D03  or another course that is approved by a departmental counselor as equivalent to ECON 2B03

name: Mathematical Economics
description: An introduction to the application of mathematics in economic theory. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: A grade of at least B- in each of ECON 2Z03  and ECON 2HH3 (or 2Y03 )

name: International Monetary Economics
description: Macroeconomic problems of an open economy with special reference to Canada; the international financial system and proposals for its reform. Three hours (lectures and seminars); one term
prerequisites: ECON 2H03 or 2Y03

name: International Trade
description: Real theory of international trade; interregional and international specialization; effect of commercial and industrial policies. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03

name: Monetary Economics
description: Introduction to a modern treatment of monetary theory. Topics include why does money exist; links between monetary policy, inflation and business cycles; how might inflation and economic growth be connected? Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03 ; and ECON 2H03 or 2Y03

name: Introduction to Game Theory
description: An introduction to the theory of games, including strategic, extensive and coalitional games. Applications in economics, political science and evolutionary biology are discussed. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 1B03
1BX3
or ARTSSCI 2E03 ; and MATH 1K03  (or equivalent)
restrictions: Not open to students with credit in ECON 3Y03 if the topic was Introduction to Game Theory.

name: The Economics of Aging
description: Topics include the macroeconomics of population aging and its impact on national pension and health plans and the microeconomics of retirement and income security. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03 ; and ECON 2H03 or 2Y03

name: Industrial Organization
description: A study of the structure, conduct and performance of industrial markets. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03

name: Economic Development
description: Topics may include the measurement of structural change, dual economies, agriculture and production, technical and institutional change, and health and nutrition. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03

name: Natural Resources
description: Competitive and socially optimal management of nonrenewable resources; market failure as illustrated by mineral cartels, fisheries and forestry, including analysis of bioeconomic models. Three hours (lectures and seminars); one term
prerequisites: One of ECON 2Z03  or ECON 2J03

name: Selected Topics
description: Topics will vary from year to year depending on student interests and faculty availability. Students should consult the Department on topics to be offered. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03  and ECON 2H03 or 2Y03

name: Health Economics
description: Analysis of allocation of resources in health care. Topics include markets for health care, insurance, biomedical research, technology assessment, organization and public policy. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03 . ECON 2B03  or another course in statistics is recommended

name: Honours Economic Analysis
description: Students discuss papers on a theme that is specific to each section and write short paper reviews and policy briefs on current economic issues. Three hours (seminars); one term
prerequisites: ECON 4F03  or ECON 4FF3 ; and ECON 3E03 or ECON 3EE3 ; and ECON 2ZZ3
and ECON 2HH3 (or ECON 2YY3 ); and enrolment in level IV of an Honours Economics Program

name: Economic Specialist Seminar
description: Under the supervision of a faculty member students present and discuss papers and write a paper presenting original research. 3 hours; one term
prerequisites: ECON 4FF3  with a grade of at least B-
and ECON 3EE3  with a grade of at least B-; or ECON 3E03 with a grade of at least A-
and an average of at least 6 in ECON 2H03 and 2HH3 (or 2Y03  and 2YY3 )
and enrolment in Level III or Level IV Honours Economics (Specialist Option) with a GPA of at least 6

name: Selected Topics
description: Topics will vary from year to year depending on student interests and faculty availability. Students should consult the Department on topics to be offered. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Permission of the Department

name: Methods of Inquiry in Economics
description: This course develops skills for investigating a research question in economics, through workshops (eg. writing, library, internet, data), and the subsequent application of the skills to an economic issue. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2ZZ3  and ECON 2HH3 (or 2YY3 ); Credit or registration in ECON 3E03 or ECON 3EE3
registration in Level III or Level IV of an Honours Economics program

name: Research Methods in Economics
description: Students discuss and present papers, learn research methods and write a critical review of the literature on an economic topic of their choice. 3 hours; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2ZZ3  with a grade of at least C+; and ECON 2HH3 (or 2YY3 ) with a grade of at least C+; ECON 3EE3  or a grade of at least A- in ECON 3E03; and registration in Level III or Level IV of an Honours Economics program with a GPA of at least 6

name: Econometrics II
description: Development of regression models appropriate to economics. Illustrations from applied micro- and macroeconomics. Three lectures; one tutorial; one term
prerequisites: ECON 2Z03  and ECON 2H03 (or 2Y03 ); and at least B- in ECON 3EE3  or at least A- in ECON 3E03 or another course that is approved by the department

name: Directed Research I
description: A reading and/or research program supervised by a Department member. A major paper is required. Interested students should consult the Department concerning admission.
prerequisites: Permission of the Department

name: Directed Research II
description: As per ECON 4M06 A/B S .
prerequisites: Permission of the Department

name: Advanced Economic Theory I
description: Mathematically oriented approaches to the analysis of the behaviour of individual consumers, workers and firms. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: A grade of at least C in one of ECON 3G03
MATH 2MC3
MATH 2X03
MATH 2XA3 ; and a grade of at least B- in ECON 2ZZ3  and ECON 2HH3 (or 2YY3 )

name: Advanced Economic Theory II
description: Analysis of dynamic macroeconomic models including models of endogenous growth and other selected topics. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: A grade of at least C in one of ECON 3G03
MATH 2MC3
MATH 2X03
MATH 2XA3 ; and a grade of at least B- in ECON 2ZZ3  and ECON 2HH3 (or 2YY3 )

name: Entrepreneurial Discovery I
description: Students learn to spot problems worth solving through industry immersion, customer observation, and beginners-mind inquiry. Core skills include opportunity framing, basic market sizing, and structured customer interviews. Short workshops introduce problem statements and simple experiment design. Students work individually or in teams and receive peer and mentor feedback. Deliverables include a validated problem statement, interview log, and insight briefs. Lectures, discussion (three hours)

name: Entrepreneurial Discovery II
description: Building on ENTREP 1EN3 , students generate, compare, and refine solution concepts. Emphasis is on value proposition design, early feasibility checks, ethics and data stewardship basics, and evidence-based iteration. Targeted workshops, field trips, and case discussions support rapid tests and reflection. Students synthesize findings into an initial concept and plan. Deliverables include an initial value proposition, experiment results summary, and a go/no-go memo with next-term milestones. Lectures, discussion (three hours)
prerequisites: ENTREP 1EN3  or INNOVATE 1X03

name: Venture Building and Business Structuring I
description: Students turn concepts into testable solutions and formalize early business models. Focus areas include prototyping or MVP v0, testing critical assumptions with target users, and early channel trials. Students explore team formation, IP and legal foundations with clinics on incorporation options. Mentors provide stage-based guidance. Deliverables include a prototype or service blueprint, test results with iteration rationale, a team charter, and an initial operating outline. Lectures, discussion (three hours)
prerequisites: Registration in the Minor of Entrepreneurship

name: Venture Building and Business Structuring II
description: Students advance to MVP v1 and prepare for a structured pilot or launch. Topics include basic financial modeling, simple unit economics, data stewardship, and ethics in operation; students refine channels and customer success practices. Field visits and mentor clinics connect ventures to ecosystem partners. By terms end, students present an MVP ready for pilot or a registered venture with an operating plan. Deliverables include an operating plan, milestone roadmap, and identified mentor network for ENTREP 3EN6 . Lectures, discussion (three hours)
prerequisites: ENTREP 2EN3 ; and registration in the Minor of Entrepreneurship

name: New Venture Operation and Strategic Pivoting
description: Focusing on market entry and operational resilience, this course guides students through launching, tracking, and adapting their business. Students build lightweight marketing, sales, and logistics plans while developing key performance metrics and dashboards. Special attention is given to recognizing when a pivot is necessary, designing new business models, and communicating pivots to stakeholders. Workshops cover pricing, unit economics, customer success, and risk management, with scenario drills and concise post-mortems. Deliverables include KPI trends, a pivot-or-persevere review grounded in product-market fit evidence, and a revised operating playbook. Lectures, discussion (three hours)
prerequisites: ENTREP 2EX3 ; and registration in the Minor of Entrepreneurship

name: Entrepreneurial Growth and Capital Acquisition
description: This capstone centers on achieving traction, scaling operations, and preparing for investment. Students analyze readiness for fundraising, develop financial plans, and craft investor pitches and supporting documents. Growth topics include hiring, culture building, governance, and engaging ecosystem partners. Financing content spans capital needs by milestone, non-dilutive options, angel and VC instruments, and data room preparation, with legal and compliance considerations for scaling. Graduates exit the course with an investor- and partner-ready growth plan, measurable 12- to 18month targets, and a clear approach to managing investor relations. Lectures, discussion (three hours)
prerequisites: ENTREP 3EN6 ; and registration in the Minor of Entrepreneurship

name: Foundations of Equitable Activity, Mobility, and Community Health
description: Explore how equity, diversity, inclusion, and accessibility (EDIA) shape physical activity, mobility, and community health. Students connect theory to practice by examining real-world applications in six PACE community exercise programs (MacPLAY, MacSeniors, MacCardiac Rehab, MacWarriors, MacMS-FITT, MacWheelers). Students examine how evidence-based practice and inclusive design improve health outcomes among community members experiencing chronic diseases and physical disabilities. Students will complete six hours of online modules with accompanying content quizzes, a facilitated small-group discussion (4-5 students; virtual), and a two-page written reflection. The course will be evaluated on a Pass/Fail basis. Web modules (six hours total); one term
prerequisites: None

name: Professionalism in Equitable Activity, Mobility, and Community Health
description: Develop professional skills alongside exercise professionals including Registered Kinesiologists and Physiotherapists while gaining practical experience promoting equity, diversity, inclusion, and accessibility (EDIA) in physical activity, mobility, and community health. Through a supervised placement at the McMaster Physical Activity Centre of Excellence (PACE), students hone communication, leadership, and person-centred delivery competencies. This hands-on learning environment connects research with professional practice in neurological, cardiac, cancer, and mobility-focused rehabilitation and community wellness. Applications are available on the Kinesiology Department website and must be submitted to the Academic Program Advisor 30 days prior to the start of the term (see Sessional Dates in the Undergraduate Calendar). Students are required to complete two hours of online modules with accompanying content quizzes and attend a two-hour in-person orientation session. A 60-hour supervised volunteer placement in PACE provides the primary experiential learning component. Placement (60 hours across PACE programs, equivalent to one day per week); web modules (two hours total); in-person orientation (two hours total); one term
prerequisites: PACE 1A01 ; current Standard First Aid/CPR/AED certification

name: Applied Practice in Equitable Activity, Mobility, and Community Health
description: Advanced skills in client engagement, clinical reasoning, and complex problem-solving. Through a supervised placement at the McMaster Physical Activity Centre of Excellence (PACE), students refine professional competencies in delivering equitable, high-quality exercise and rehabilitation programming for clients with diverse abilities and backgrounds. Applications are available on the Kinesiology Department website and must be submitted to the Academic Program Advisor 30 days prior to the start of the term (see Sessional Dates in the Undergraduate Calendar). Students are required to complete two hours of online modules with accompanying content quizzes and attend a two-hour in-person orientation session. Students will complete a 60-hour supervised volunteer placement in PACE as the primary experiential learning component. Placement (60 hours across PACE programs, equivalent to one day per week); web modules (two hours total); in-person orientation (two hours total); one term
prerequisites: PACE 2A03 ; current Standard First Aid/CPR/AED certification

name: Advanced Practice in Equitable Activity, Mobility, and Community Health
description: A non-credit capstone experience recognizing the completion of an additional 60 volunteer hours beyond PACE 3A03 . Completion of this course fulfills the final requirement for the Microcredential in Equitable Activity, Mobility, and Community Health (180 total hours), which will be formally noted on the student transcript.
prerequisites: PACE 3A03 ; current Standard First Aid/CPR/AED Certification

name: Communication Systems
description: Signal and system representations, Fourier transform and LTI systems, filtering; analog communication systems: amplitude modulation, frequency modulation and phase modulation; digital communication systems: pulse modulation, digital transmission at baseband, digital modulation techniques: amplitude-shift keying, phase-shift keying, and frequency-shift keying. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3MA3  and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Transmission Lines and Electromagnetics
description: Formerly ENRTECH 4EM3 Field concepts. Maxwells equations, integral and differential forms. Free space and guided wave propagation, transmission lines. Radiation from current elements. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3MA3  and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Power Systems and Electrical Machines
description: Basic electric circuits, basic electrical theorems, network analysis, phasors, three phase systems, transformers, motors, electric power generation, power plants components (transformers, motors, exciters, synchronous machines). Three lectures; one lab (two hours every other week); one term
prerequisites: Registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Industrial Networks and Communication Systems
description: Corporate and industrial network standards; proprietary buses and protocols and interfaces; distributed I/O; drivers and devices and their implementation in PC and PLC based systems. Three lectures; one lab (two hours every other week); one term
prerequisites: Registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Measurements and Instrumentation
description: Transducers, logic circuits, basic electronic devices and their applications. Calculate/ measure the input(s) and output(s) of various systems. Recognize, install and apply instruments within power plants. Three lectures; one lab (two hours every other week); one term
prerequisites: Registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Power Distribution I
description: Principle concepts and theories of power distribution. Skills required to work at an industrial environment and/or power utilities (generation, transmission, distribution). Based on the Ontario Hydro system, a power flow computer program will be introduced. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENRTECH 3EP3  and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Computer Applications in Power System Engineering
description: Analysis of load flow, short circuit, transient stability and electromagnetic transients by commercial power system software packages. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3ET0
ENRTECH 3PD3
4PM3
and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Power System Analysis and Control
description: This course introduces the different types of operating constraints as encountered by power system operators and engineers during real time operation of interconnected power grids. For each type of operating constraint, the most common operating strategies and control measures will be discussed and analyzed. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENRTECH 3PD3  and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Power Electronics
description: Introduction to power semiconductor switching devices: power diodes, thyristors, IGBTs, MOSFETs; four types of converters in power conditioning: DC-DC, DC-AC, AC-DC, and AC-AC. Applications of power electronics in electric power transmission and distribution: static var compensators (SVCs), static synchronous condensers (STATCOM), voltage source converters (VSC) and HVDC transmission. Lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENRTECH 3EP3
ENGTECH 3MA3
ENRTECH 3PD3
and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Power Protection and Maintenance I
description: Various power devices such as relays, circuit breaker, power monitor, control devices and other components used in a power system protection. Other devices such as CTs, and Pts and substation hardware will also be covered. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENRTECH 3MI3
3PD3
and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Power Protection and Maintenance II
description: New generation of digital fault detection systems. Balanced faults, computer-based fault studies, symmetrical components and sequence networks, unbalanced short-circuit and open-circuit faults. Three lectures; one lab (two hours every other week); one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3ET0
ENRTECH 4PM3  and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Renewable Generation
description: Operation and planning of renewable generation resources including wind, solar, hydro, biomass, geothermal and fuel cells. The environmental and economical impacts of such technologies, rules, regulations. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENRTECH 3EP3
ENGTECH 3TD3
and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Introduction to Career Planning & Employment
description: Introduction to career readiness and job search; self-assessment, career planning and decision-making, networking, industry research, cover letter and resume writing, interviewing skills and work place professionalism.
prerequisites: Registration in B.Eng
B.A.Sc
B.Eng.Mgt
B.Eng.Soc
B.Eng.BioSci
B.Tech 4-YR Not open to students in their final level
restrictions: Not open to students in their final level.

name: Integrated Cornerstone Design Projects in Engineering
description: Project-based integrated learning course that introduces a range of foundational (i.e., cornerstone) topics in engineering, including engineering design and communication, computation, graphic design, natural and applied sciences, sustainability and the engineering profession. These topics are applied through a series of integrated team-based design projects in simulated workplace environments. Three lectures, one tutorial (two hours), two labs (three hours each); both terms
prerequisites: Registration in any Engineering program
restrictions: Antirequisite(s): ENGINEER 1C03, ENGINEER 1D04, ENGINEER 1P03, ENGINEER 1PA3 , ENGINEER 1PB3 , ENGINEER 1PC3 , IBEHS 1P10 A/B , MATLS 1M03

name: Introduction to Engineering Design and Practice
description: Introduction to professional engineering including ethics, health and safety, engineering communication; design skills; completion of a design project. Graphical visualization and communication; technical sketching, 2D and 3D computer-aided design; use of solid modelling software. Two lectures, one tutorial (two hours); one term
prerequisites: Registration in any Engineering program
and permission of the department
restrictions: Antirequisite(s): ENGINEER 1P13 A/B , IBEHS 1P10 A/B , ENGINEER 1C03

name: Structure and Properties of Materials
description: An introduction to the structure of both crystalline and amorphous solids; the physical and chemical basis for properties exhibited by materials; an overview of material properties including mechanical, electrical, magnetic and thermal behaviour. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: Registration in any Engineering program
and permission of the department
restrictions: Antirequisite(s): ENGINEER 1P13 A/B , IBEHS 1P10 A/B , MATLS 1M03

name: Engineering Computation
description: Development and analysis of simple algorithms. Implementation of algorithms in computer programming language. Design and testing of computer programs. One lecture, one tutorial (two hours), one lab (three hours); one term
prerequisites: Registration in any Engineering program
and permission of the department
restrictions: Antirequisite(s): ENGINEER 1P13 A/B , IBEHS 1P10 A/B , ENGINEER 1D04

name: Engineering Work Term
description: Minimum of 12 weeks of full-time employment in a professional environment. First or second term
prerequisites: Registration in a Co-op program in the Faculty of Engineering and ENGINEER 1EE0  and permission from the Engineering Co-Op and Career Services
restrictions: Not open to students in their final level.

name: Inclusion in the Engineering Workplace
description: Engineering workplaces are diverse but can pose challenges to underrepresented groups. Students will develop the vocabulary and tools to master perceptual, institutional, and psychological mechanisms of inclusion as allies and targets. One term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II

name: Engineering: Communications and Social Impact
description: A multidisciplinary integrated learning course focused on communication and the engineering design cycle. Formal and informal, verbal and written communication skills are fostered through project work. Two lectures, one tutorial (two hours); second term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above in any program leading to a B.Eng
or B.Eng.Biosci. Not open to the Engineering and Management or Engineering and Society programs
restrictions: Antirequisite(s): CHEMENG 2G03; CIVENG 2I03; COMPENG 2DX4; ENGPHYS 3EC4; MECHENG 2A03; MATLS 2H04; SFWRENG 3I03, ENGSOCTY 2X03, ENGNMGT 2AA3

name: Emerging Leaders and Mentors
description: This workshop-based course offers students the opportunity to earn course credit for their leadership and mentorship roles within the McMaster community and beyond. Participants will receive training in various aspects of mentorship and leadership, enhancing their current skills and fostering personal and professional growth. Students must coordinate with the course instructor prior to enrollment. One lecture (three hours); both terms
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program and permission of the instructor

name: Full-Time Internship for International Students
description: Full-time, paid internships of 8, 12 or 16 months enable international Engineering students to explore career opportunities and work environments, gain employability skills, and an understanding of employer expectations and employment practices in a Canadian professional work environment.
prerequisites: ENGINEER 1EE0  and permission of the Engineering Career and Co-Op Services

name: Engineering Economics
description: Engineering economic analysis explored in the context of an interdisciplinary engineering project. Students perform cost-benefit analysis considering the perspective of the engineering team, client, and society in order to maximize net value of an engineering decision. Factors considered and incorporated include conversion factors, opportunity cost, time value of money, risk analysis, and technical analysis. Two lectures, one tutorial (two hours); second term
prerequisites: ENGINEER 2PX3  or ENGSOCTY 2X03  or ENGNMGT 2AA3 ; Registration in Level III or above in any program leading to a B.Eng
B.Eng.Mgt
or a B.Eng.Soc degree

name: Ethics, Equity and Law in Engineering
description: General introduction to the ethical, equitable and legal aspects of engineering practice. Topics include the engineering act and code of ethics, employment equity, legal duties and liabilities of the professional engineer, contracts, and the tort of negligence. Three lectures; one term, offered both fall and winter
prerequisites: Registration in Level IV or above of any Engineering program or credit or registration in a six-unit Engineering capstone course. Not open to students in the Engineering & Society program

name: Experiential Engineering Design
description: This course will provide students an opportunity for formal recognition of the design-based experiential learning conducted within the atmosphere of technically-oriented McMaster Engineering teams. Arrangements for participation in this course must be made with the course instructor prior to enrolment. One lecture (three hours); both terms
prerequisites: Registration in Level III

name: Inquiry in an Engineering Context I
description: Inquiry is a non-disciplinary approach to the study of issues of public concern. In terms of the design process, inquiry focuses on the problem definition stage, in which formulating questions, researching underlying issues, and analysing opposing arguments are essential. The first course involves teaching how to use the university and community resources in research, how to write a research paper, and how to express ideas orally. Three hours (lectures, discussion, group work); first term
prerequisites: Registration in the Engineering and Society Program or permission of the instructor

name: Case Studies in History and Technology
description: History and philosophy of technology, from antiquity to modern times, with a special emphasis on the cultural aspects of technology, are addressed on a case study basis. Three hours (lectures, discussion, group work); second term
prerequisites: Registration in the Engineering and Society Program

name: Inquiry in an Engineering Context II
description: This inquiry course builds on the skills developed in previous courses, focusing on a specific issue related to the role of engineering and technology in society. The course is devoted to the study of one topic such as: social control of technology, technology and the quality of life, the deteriorating environment, or the information society. Three hours (lectures, discussion, group presentations); second term
prerequisites: ENGSOCTY 2X03  and registration in Level IV of the Engineering and Society Program

name: Technology and Society
description: A study of the nature and structure of technology, the nature of culture, and the role and place of different groups, including engineers, in a culture dominated by technology; and mechanisms for the social control of technology. Lectures, discussion, group work, seminars (three hours); first term
prerequisites: ENGSOCTY 2Y03  and registration in Level III or above of the Engineering and Society Program

name: Preventive Engineering: Environmental Perspectives
description: This experiential course focuses on the application of preventive engineering with specific attention to impacts on the natural environment. Students explore first-hand, through guided site visits and discussion with organizational leaders, the potential solutions and risks of this approach Three hours (lectures, discussion, group projects); first term
prerequisites: Registration in Level III or IV of the Engineering and Society Program

name: Inquiry in an Engineering Context III
description: Under the supervision of a faculty member, students write an inquiry paper and present their findings orally. Topics for inquiry must bear on the relation of technology to society and have implications for the practising engineer. One lecture (three hours); both terms
prerequisites: ENGSOCTY 3X03  and registration in Level V of the Engineering and Society Program

name: Society Capstone Design
description: In multi-disciplinary teams, students will complete a capstone design project that incorporates holistic design, social sustainability, community resilience and aesthetic elements. Two lectures; design studio (one hour); first term
prerequisites: Registration in Level V of the Engineering and Society Program

name: Communication Skills
description: Writing skills including formal reports; speaking, listening and presentation skills, speeches, technical presentations and electronic communication technology. One lecture (three hours); first term
prerequisites: Registration in the Engineering and Management program

name: Leading High-Performance Engineering Teams
description: This course explores the principles and practices of effective team leadership within engineering and management contexts. Students will learn how to build and lead high-performance teams through topics such as team dynamics, communication strategies, conflict resolution, and fostering innovation. One lecture (three hours); second term
prerequisites: ENGNMGT 2AA3  and registration in Level III or above in the Engineering and Management program

name: Innovation Driven Project Development and Management
description: What is innovation and how is it managed? Team-based creativity skills will be developed with a focus on delivering innovation. Participants develop teamwork skills while using project management tools to develop a project. One lecture (three hours); first term
prerequisites: One of CHEMENG 2G03 or ENGNMGT 2AA2 or ENGNMGT 2AA3  or ENGNMGT 3A03 ; and registration in Level IV or above in the Engineering and Management program

name: Engineering and Management Capstone
description: Capstone course: Students work in multidisciplinary teams to solve an integrated engineering and business problem in an organization. Team, project and client management skills are developed. One lecture (three hours); first term
prerequisites: ENGNMGT 4A03  and registration in the Engineering and Management program

name: Analytical Chemistry
description: Introduction to laboratory procedures used in chemical analysis for classical wet and instrumental methods; statistical data treatment, gravimetric analysis, volumetric analysis, pH measurements and optical methods. Three lectures, one lab (three hours); second term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 1CH3  and registration in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program or the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: Biology
description: This course provides basic introduction to the following topics: chemistry of life, cells, genetics, evolution and diversity and plant and animal form and function. Two lectures, one lab (three hours every other week); second term
prerequisites: Registration in the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: Chemistry
description: Basic chemical concepts, calculations and laboratory procedures. Chemical formulae and equations, chemical stoichiometry, nomenclature, acids and bases, gases, chemical equilibrium, thermochemistry and thermodynamics, redox reactions and electrochemistry. Two lectures, two tutorials, one lab (three hours every other week); first term
prerequisites: Registration in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: C++ Programming
description: Programming concepts and introduction to C++ programming. C++ syntax, functions, decision-making, looping, pointers, and arrays, strings, data structures, and file operations. Two lectures, one lab (two hours); first term
prerequisites: Registration in the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Electricity and Circuit Analysis
description: Introduction to electronic circuits; DC and AC sources, resistors, inductors, and capacitors; phasors and impedance; transient and steady-state analysis; network analysis; energy and power. Two lectures, two tutorials, one lab (three hours); second term
prerequisites: Registration in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the  Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: Introduction to the Technology Co-op Program
description: Orientation to Technology Co-op programs and the workplace; self-assessment and goal setting; application procedures and materials; occupational health and safety.
prerequisites: Registration in a Degree Completion Technology Co-op program

name: Mathematics I
description: Pre-calculus concepts: algebra, trigonometry, complex numbers, exponential and logarithmic functions, systems of equations, matrices, determinants and vectors. Limits, continuity, differential calculus, partial derivatives, applications, sequences and series. Two lectures, two tutorials; first term
prerequisites: Registration in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: Statics and Mechanics of Materials
description: Statics and kinematics of particles and rigid bodies: force vectors; equilibrium; trusses, frames and machines; internal forces; centroids; friction; axial load, torsion, bending and shear; stress and strain. Newton’s Second Law; moments of inertia; plane motion. Four lectures; second term
prerequisites: Registration in the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Mathematics II
description: Integral calculus involving all the techniques of integration, applications, improper integrals, multiple integrals and integral theorems, infinite sequences and series. Two lectures, two tutorials; second term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 1MC3  and registration in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: Principles and Applications of Object-Oriented Programming
description: A project-based computer programming course that covers pointers, structured data types, and object-oriented principles, including inheritance, polymorphism, abstract classes, and function overloading. Two lectures, one lab (two hours); second term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 1PP3  and registration in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Physics
description: Sound, light, kinematics, forces, work, energy, fluid and thermal physics. Four lectures, one lab (two hours every other week); first term
prerequisites: Registration in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: Programming Fundamentals
description: Introduction to programming concepts using Python, including syntax, functions, decision-making, and looping. Topics also cover operators, arrays, and fundamental data structures for problem-solving and application development. Two lectures, one lab (two hours); first term
prerequisites: Registration in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program or the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: Object-Oriented Programming
description: Project-based course covering computer programming. Pointers, structured data, object-oriented concepts, inheritance, polymorphism, abstract class and overloading functions. Two lectures, one lab (two hours); second term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 1CP3  and registration in the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Four Month Co-op Experience I
description: Minimum of 12 weeks of full-time employment in a professional environment.
prerequisites: ENGINEER 1EE0  and registration in a Four-Year Technology Program and permission of the Engineering Co-op and Career Services Office

name: Engineering Statistics
description: An introductory statistics course covering the following topics with engineering applications: organization and description of data, probability and distributions, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing and bivariate data analysis using regression. Two lectures, one tutorial; first term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 1MT3 ; and registration in the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Four Month Co-op Experience I
description: Minimum of 12 weeks of full-time employment in a professional environment.
prerequisites: ENGTECH 1ET0
registration in a Degree Completion Technology Co-op program
and permission of the Engineering Co-op and Career Services Office

name: Mathematics III
description: Techniques for solving first and second order ordinary differential equations with applications; initial value and boundary value problems, systems of differential equations, partial differential equations. Two lectures, two tutorials; first term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 1MT3 ; and registration in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program
the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: Modelling and Numerical Solutions
description: Number systems and errors; solutions to nonlinear equations; interpolation by polynomials; matrices and systems of linear equations; numerical integration; spline functions, differential equations; engineering applications. Two lectures, one tutorial; second term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 1CP3
ENGTECH 1MT3 ; and registration in the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Mathematics IV
description: Continuous time signals and systems; convolution; Laplace transform, Fourier series and transform; Discrete time signals and systems. Two lectures, two tutorials; second term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 2MA3 ; and registration in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program or the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Discrete Mathematics
description: Fundamental discrete mathematics concepts relevant to IT: sets, relations, functions, graphs, propositional logic. State machines. Input/output specifications. Invariants. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: Registration in the Software Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Four Month Co-op Experience II
description: Minimum of 12 weeks of full-time employment in a professional environment. First term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 2EE0 ; registration in a Four-Year Technology Program; and permission of the Engineering Co-op and Career Services Office Cannot be taken concurrently with any program capstone course

name: Engineering Statistics
description: An introductory statistics course covering the following topics with engineering applications: organization and description of data, probability and distributions, confidence intervals and hypothesis testing and bivariate data analysis using regression. Two lectures, one tutorial; first term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 1MT3 ; and registration in Level III of the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program or the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: Four Month Co-op Experience II
description: Minimum of 12 weeks of full-time employment in a professional environment.
prerequisites: ENGTECH 2ET0
registration in a Degree Completion Technology Co-op program
and permission of the Engineering Co-op and Career Services Office

name: Finite Element Analysis
description: Matrix techniques; eigenvalue problems: equations of elasticity: plane stress, plane strain, 3D problems; variational methods; element types, element stiffness, mass matrices and load vector; assemblage of elements, boundary conditions. Three lectures; first term
prerequisites: AUTOTECH 2AC3
AUTOTECH 2TS3
and registration in Level III of the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Mathematics V
description: Ordinary and partial differential equations; Laplace transforms; Fourier series; vector calculus; integral theorems, with engineering applications. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: Registration in the Civil Engineering Infrastructure Technology Co-op program
the Manufacturing Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Strength of Materials
description: Stresses under combined loads, generalized Hooke’s Law; two and three dimensional stresses, stress transformation, principal stresses, Mohr’s circle; deflections by integration; energy methods, Castagliano’s theorem; columns; yield criteria. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3MA3
3SD3
and registration in the Civil Engineering Infrastructure Technology Co-op program or the Manufacturing Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Modelling and Numerical Solutions
description: Number systems and errors; solutions to nonlinear equations; interpolation by polynomials; matrices and systems of linear equations; differentiation and integration; differential equations; applications to mechanical systems. Two lectures, one tutorial; first term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 1CP3
ENGTECH 2MA3 ; and registration in Level IV or above of the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Statics and Dynamics
description: Two and three dimensional force vectors, equilibrium of a particle; moments and couples; equilibrium rigid bodies; centroids, second moment of area, moment of inertia; truss, and static analysis. Planar kinematics and planar kinetics of particles and rigid bones; work and energy, impulse, and momentum. Two lectures, one lab; one term
prerequisites: Registration in the Civil Engineering Infrastructure Technology Co-op program or the Manufacturing Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Structure and Properties of Materials
description: Structure of crystalline solids; imperfections in solids; mechanical properties of metals, dislocations and strengthening mechanisms, failure, phase diagrams, phase transformation in metals, processing of metal alloys, composites, structures and properties of ceramics, processing of ceramics. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: Registration in the Civil Engineering Infrastructure Technology Co-op program or the Manufacturing Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Probability and Statistics
description: Probability and statistics for engineering and technology. Descriptive statistics, discrete and continuous random variables and probability distributions, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, analysis of variance, correlation and regression. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3MA3  and registration in the Civil Engineering Infrastructure Technology Co-op program

name: Thermodynamics
description: Introduction to thermodynamics, properties of pure substances, first and second laws of thermodynamics, entropy, vapor power cycles, refrigeration cycles, and combined power cycles. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: Registration in the Manufacturing Engineering Technology Co-op program or the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Artificial Intelligence
description: Theories and practice of machine intelligence with focus on statistical learning methods, artificial neural networks, naturally inspired algorithms, deep learning, big data management, and pattern recognition. Three lectures, one term; completely virtual
prerequisites: Registration in level IV of the Biotechnology Co-op program
the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program

OR Registration in the Manufacturing Engineering Technology Co-op program or the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program OR MECHENG 4R03  or IBEHS 4A03  and registration in any Mechanical Engineering Program

name: Systems and Control
description: Mathematical models of physical systems; differential equations, Laplace transforms; block diagrams, transfer functions; system transient response; stability analysis in s-, frequency-, and time-domain; Routh-Hurwitz criteria, root-locus analysis, Bode plots, Nyquist criterion, state-space representation; simple PID control systems; lead-lag compensation; digital simulations of control systems. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3MA3  and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program or the Manufacturing Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Engineering Design & Technology
description: This course provides students with formal recognition of engineering design and technology skills acquired through experiential learning in technically oriented McMaster Engineering Teams. Permission of course instructor is required prior to enrolment. One lecture (3 hours), fall term
prerequisites: Registration in Level 3 or above in the Automation Systems Engineering Technology Co-op program or the Automotive and Vehicle Engineering Technology Co-op program
or the Biotechnology Co-op program

name: Senior Engineering Design Project
description: A project involving design and synthesis that reinforces concepts gained from previous semesters. Such a project involves research, design, and assessment. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3ET0
CIVTECH 4SD3  or 4RC3 ; and registration in Level IV of the Civil Engineering Infrastructure Technology Co-op program

name: Four Month Co-op Experience III
description: Minimum of 12 weeks of full-time employment in a professional environment.
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3EE0 ; registration in a Four-Year Technology Program; and permission of the Engineering Co-op and Career Services Office

name: Senior Engineering Project
description: A project that is based on the knowledge gained from previous semesters. Such a project involves research, design, development and implementation of a process. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3ET0
4CT3
4PD3
4PM3
and registration in the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Finite Element Analysis
description: Formerly ENGTECH 3FA3. Matrix techniques, eigenvalue problems, equation of elasticity, 3D problems, variational methods, element types, element stiffness, mass matrix and load vector, assemblage of elements, boundary conditions. Two lectures, one lab; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3ML3  and ENGTECH 4MA3  or CIVTECH 3MN3
and registration in the Civil Engineering Infrastructure Technology Co-op program or the Manufacturing Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Senior Engineering Project
description: Project-based course using the agglomeration of previously acquired knowledge. Research, design, implement and document a software solution to a problem in a real-world application domain. Three lectures, one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3ET0 ; and
21 units of ENGTECH and SFWRTECH at level 3; and
18 units of SFWRTECH from level 4; and
registration in Level IV Software Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Advanced Mathematics
description: Sequence and series, Fourier series, Matrix algebra, Formulating engineering process models, Numerical solutions techniques, Root findings, Curve fittings, Numerical integration, Numerical differentiation, Ordinary differential equations. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3MA3  and registration in the Civil Engineering Infrastructure Technology Co-op program
the Manufacturing Engineering Technology Co-op program or the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Mechanics of Fluids
description: Fluid statics, flow in closed conduits, dimensional analysis and similarity, energy and Bernoulli’s equation, flow kinematics, hydraulic cross-sections, energy loss in piping system, fluid Machinery. Three lectures, one lab; one term
prerequisites: ENGTECH 3MA3  and registration in the Civil Engineering Infrastructure Technology Co-op program
the Manufacturing Engineering Technology Co-op program or the Power and Energy Engineering Technology Co-op program

name: Studying Culture: A Critical Introduction
description: The course will introduce fundamental concepts and questions in the field of cultural studies, and will prepare students to use those tools in analyzing culture as a site of meaning, identities, power, and pleasure. The course aims to develop your ability to think critically about your own engagements with a broad range of manifestations of culture (e.g. popular culture, social institutions, everyday practices, digital culture, consumer culture). Considerable emphasis will be placed on the development of critical skills in reading and writing. Two lectures, one tutorial; one term

name: The Written World
description: What does the world look like when it takes a literary form? We will read and write about one or more literary genres or forms from various times and places, and reflect on the shape of literature, its place in the world, and the place of the world in it. The course functions as an introduction to the study of literature, equipping students with conceptual, analytical and writing tools that will help them become informed readers of the many modes and manners of imaginative expression. Considerable emphasis will be placed on the development of critical skills in reading and writing. Two lectures, one tutorial; one term

name: Making and Unmaking Literary Traditions
description: This introductory course explores literatures written in English from the perspective of literary historical periods, genres, and critical approaches. We will trace how particular literary traditions emerge in relation to developments in the cultural narratives of, for example, gender and sexuality, selfhood, nation and empire, capitalism, and the environment. We will consider how a literary text is an expression of a particular cultural moment, with all its social and material preoccupations, and yet makes meaning through a complex dialogue with past traditions. The course functions as an introduction to the study of literature, equipping students with conceptual, analytical, and writing tools that will help them become an informed reader of the many modes and manners of imaginative expression. Considerable emphasis will be placed on the development of critical skills in reading and writing. Two lectures, one tutorial; one term

name: Words in Place
description: Many public ceremonies in Canada now include acknowledgements of whose land we are meeting on. What does it mean to acknowledge the people and the place where we live and work? How do places come into focus when we write and speak about them? This introductory course examines oral narratives, art, poetry, film, documentary, fiction, and/or literary non-fiction that emphasize the dynamics of particular places in relation to Indigenous and colonial histories; diasporic histories of movement, displacement, emigration and immigration; natural, economic, and political geographies; as well as the particular languages – i.e. different Englishes, Indigenous languages – that places give rise to. Considerable emphasis will be placed on the development of critical skills in reading and writing. Two lectures, one tutorial; one term

name: Literature and Culture in the United States
description: A study of literary and cultural production in the United States, focusing on selected movements, issues, genres or traditions. Eg. Seventeenth century first-encounter narratives, post-civil war reconstructions, Native American Renaissance, Asian-American literature and cinema, the Beat Generation, the Harlem Renaissance, American underground commix. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Twentieth- and Twenty-First Century British Literature and Film
description: An introduction to the twentieth- and twenty-first-century literary texts and films from the British Isles, with attention to their historical, cultural, and socio-political contexts. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Contemporary Canadian Fiction
description: A study of the themes and structure of the contemporary Canadian novel, usually with emphasis on the relationship between Canada’s cultural patterns and its literature. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program
restrictions: Not open to students with credit or registration in ENGLISH 2G06 A/B.

name: Settler Colonialism and Writing in Canada
description: This course looks at ways literary writing has contributed to and contested the formation of Canada as a settler colony. Examining a selection of literary works from the stories of European explorers to the present, this course traces how many works have provided the rationale for colonial domination of land and people in Canada, while many others have voiced resistance and imagined alternatives. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Canadian Literature of Dissent and Social Justice
description: This course critically examines the way social justice concerns in Canadian literature, film, and music have grown out of and critiqued dominant narratives about Canadas culture, makeup, and purpose. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Shakespeare: Comedies, Problem Plays, and Romances
description: A close study of selected plays in these genres, together with relevant literary, cultural, theatrical, and historical contexts. May include plays by other dramatists. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Genre in Creative Writing
description: This course combines features of a creative writing workshop with the challenges of working in literary genre. Lectures will introduce the genres available to writers, concentrating on verse forms and short narrative. Students will present installments of their own work in workshops. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Shakespeare: Histories and Tragedies
description: A close study of selected plays in these genres, together with relevant literary, cultural, theatrical, and historical contexts. May include plays by other dramatists. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Indigenous Futurisms and Wonderworks
description: Through a focus on Indigenous articulated realities and futures, this course refuses colonial narratives of the ‘disappearing Indian’ and insists upon Indigenous presence in past, present, and future as essential for envisioning a human future. Genres of study will include fiction, graphic novels, film, non-fiction, performance, and wonderworks.
prerequisites: One of INDIGST 1A03
1AA3
RECONCIL 1A03; or three units of Level I English; or permission of the Instructor

name: Studies in Women Writers
description: A closely focused course on women’s writing in English. The topic for the course varies, sometimes concentrating on specific issues, sometimes on an historical period or national literature. Relevant feminist theory will be a component of the course. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program
restrictions: Antirequisite(s): CSCT 2K06 A/B, CSCT 2KK3, ENGLISH 2K06 A/B, WOMENST 2K06 A/B, 2KK3

name: Concepts of Culture
description: An analysis of the concept of culture from the Enlightenment to the present. Theoretical readings combined with the analysis of specific cultural texts, objects, forms, and practices will allow students to trace historical and contemporary debates concerning culture. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program
restrictions: Antirequisite(s): ARTHIST 2M03, CMST 2M03, CSCT 2M03, CSCT 2M06 A/B, ENGLISH 2M06 A/B

name: Popular Culture
description: This course examines the study of everyday culture, its underlying assumptions, its locations, and the capacity of audiences to engage actively and critically with it. Possible areas of study may include: advertising, fandom, film, TV, social media, youth culture, celebrity, memes, comics, online apps, popular music, video. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Queer Writing, Art, and Activism: Reimagining the World
description: This course examines queer writing, art, and activism of the late 20th and early 21st century, with an emphasis on creative works by Black and Indigenous queer writers, artists and activists who address decolonization, abolition, and resistance. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Social Justice, Literature and the Rhetoric of Science and Technology
description: This course approaches science and technology through the lens of literary and cultural studies by analyzing the production, communication, and representation of scientific and technological knowledge through a range of written and visual texts. Critical frameworks can include science and technology studies, medical humanities, environmental humanities, cultural studies, critical disability studies, Indigenous studies, alongside feminist, queer, and critical race theories. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Literary and Cultural Studies: Theory and Practice
description: This course will offer a grounding in reading literary texts and culture from a range of contemporary critical approaches. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in a program in English and Cultural Studies

name: Topics in Visual Culture
description: This course examines visual texts in a select media and genres through an exploration of a variety of theoretical discourses and representational practices. Approaches can include cultural studies, film theories, and gender, queer, and critical race theories. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program. Not open to students with credit or registration in ENGLISH 2P03 or CSCT 2P03
if the topic is Modernity
Postmodernity
Visuality; with credit or registration in ENGLISH 2S03 or CSCT 2S03
if the topic is Spectacular Bodies; or with credit or registration in ENGLISH 3CC3
CSCT 3CC3
CMST 3CC3
THTRFLM 3R03
if the topic is Reading Film
restrictions: Not open to students with credit or registration in ENGLISH 2P03 or CSCT 2P03, if the topic is Modernity, Postmodernity, Visuality; with credit or registration in ENGLISH 2S03 or CSCT 2S03, if the topic is Spectacular Bodies; or with credit or registration in ENGLISH 3CC3, CSCT 3CC3, CMST 3CC3, THTRFLM 3R03, if the topic is Reading Film.

name: Reading Environmental Humanities
description: A study of representations of nature in a variety of written and visual texts. Topics may include food, environmental crisis, development, humans and other animals. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Critical Race Studies
description: This course examines contemporary debates in critical race theory in an attempt to critically decode the operations of race in literary and cultural texts. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level III or above in a program in English and Cultural Studies
Global Peace and Social Justice
Justice
Political Philosophy and Law
Peace Studies
or Indigenous Studies

name: Theories of Gender and Sexuality
description: This course explores a range of theories of gender and sexuality by working through readings from the intersecting fields of feminist, queer and masculinity studies. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level III or above in a program in English and Cultural Studies
or Justice
Political Philosophy and Law

name: Caribbean Literature
description: In this course we will study works by writers from the Caribbean region and its diasporas, many of which are housed in McMaster’s archives. This course introduces students to some of the Caribbean region’s best-known writers and explores their creative work and worlds. We will explore questions of race, gender, power, colonialism, decolonization and transnationalism, and the politics of writing place as well as the politics of representation and of memory. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Three units of ENGLISH and registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Writing Practices
description: This course focuses on creative writing as a practice rather than a process towards material products, exploring the relationship between habitual writing exercises and an understanding of how writing–as activity, discourse, archive–helps shape the world as we experience it. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Writing Out
description: Through a series of modules on the transition from the private world of composition to the increasingly public phases of submitting ones work for publication to the processes of editing, reviewing, copy-editing, and publication, this course walks students through the steps towards getting their work into the public realm. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in the Concurrent Certificate in Creative Writing and Narrative Arts (CWNA) or permission of the Department

name: Creating Writing in/for/with Communities
description: This creative writing inquiry class engages students in the staged development of a creative writing project in consultation with and on behalf of a community of their choice. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Enlightenment and its Shadows
description: A study of British Literature and Culture of the long eighteenth-century (1660-1800), including plays, poetry, fiction, and essays. Themes include sexual politics, consumerism, globalization, the public sphere, and subjectivity. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Topics in Popular Genres
description: This course will provide an in-depth exploration of the conventions and consumption of one or more popular genres, such as graphic narrative, science fiction, romance, horror, crime writing, fantasy, chicklit or memoir. Three lectures; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Theories of Decolonization and Resistance
description: A study of theoretical and cultural works that examine the effects of empire and chart projects for decolonization. Introduces debates in Indigenous and postcolonial studies, including as they engage with theories of racial capitalism, gender and sexuality, globalization, war, environmental change. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program
restrictions: Antirequisite(s): CSCT 3R06 A/B, ENGLISH 3R06 A/B, PEACEST 3E06 A/B, PEACEST 3GG3

name: Reading the Embodied Past: Gender and Sexuality
description: A study of representations of gender, sexuality, and/or their institutions and intimacies in pre-20th century literature and culture, with attention to their material, cultural, and socio-political contexts. Students will examine social issues through the study of early fiction, non-fiction, drama, and poetry. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Narratives of Health
description: This course inquires into representations of health with reference to a range of media. Critical frameworks may include critical disability studies, environmental humanities, feminist research, critical race studies, science and technology studies, narrative medicine, and Indigenous studies. Three hours; one term
prerequisites: Registration in Level II or above of any program

name: Indigenous Orature and Literature as Anti-Colonial Praxis, 1750-1950
